Flügel, Gustav, *Die arabischen, persischen und türkischen Handschriften der Kaiserlich-Königlichen Hofbibliothek zu Wien*, vol. 1, Vienna: Verlag der K. K. Hof- und Staatsdruckerei, 1865: 565-567.
5d9c4672-e793-561a-835c-cda69931fe09.binding_desc:
The black lacquer binding on this manuscript closes with a flap. On the spine of the flap there are verses written in gold starting with the words "in hamsa", therefore relating directly to the text of the manuscript. Because of this relation between the text and the binding it can safely be assumed that the binding was manufactured explicitly for this manuscript.  
The binding is decorated with floral motifs and golden ornamental medallions. The doublures of the manuscript are made out of brown leather and decorated with blue medallions.  
The binding is rather fragile and parts of the painted lacquer have chipped off.

5e053a64-1076-5c13-b2f5-a260eeae41de.name:
The court of Kayumars  
Folio from the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
5e053a64-1076-5c13-b2f5-a260eeae41de.short_description: Firdausi’s epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings), completed in 1010, recounts the history of all of Iran’s shahs (kings) up to the Arab conquest in 642 AD and the country’s adoption of Islam. A large part of the poem focuses on prehistoric, legendary kings, some of whom ruled for hundreds of years and established man’s knowledge of everything from fire to weaving. According to Firdausi, the very idea of kingship originated with King Kayumars, who ruled for thirty years, overseeing a peaceable kingdom in which men wore leopard-skin robes and wild animals grew tame. In this utopia Kayumars had one secret enemy, the evil Ahriman, whose envy drove him to incite his own son, the Black Div, to murder Siyamak, the son of Kayumars. Before the assassination took place, the angel Surush warned Kayumars of Ahriman’s plot.
5e053a64-1076-5c13-b2f5-a260eeae41de.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

5ff60937-5e79-50fd-9f4b-b979480be0f5.name: *A Youth with a Lion* Folio from an album
5ff60937-5e79-50fd-9f4b-b979480be0f5.short_description:
The depicted scene takes place in a garden of a Persian Shah or a lord. Only the upper elite of Iranian society could afford keeping large predatory felines in their gardens. The young man's headdress fits the AD mid-17th century Safavid fashion.  
The author of the painting is Afzal al-Husayni (also named Mir Afzal Tuni, Afzal), a younger contemporary and follower of Reza Abbasi. Known primarily as the master of erotic drawing, Afzal preferred to depict the leisure of the Persian aristocracy: young men or love scenes in the garden. In addition to the artistic manner, the author is also indicated by an inscription in the bottom right of the folio that reads: “He! On the first day of the month of Jumat the Second of year 1056, the drawing of the most humble Afzal al-Husayni was completed”.  
Since the late 16th century the Iranian miniature has acquired the role of an independent piece of art. The prestige of the artist's work and his creative and economic freedom was growing, and it became much easier to make a living on producing single page works than on illustrating a whole book. Separate paintings as well as calligraphic folios with poems constituted *murakka* albums, reflecting the aesthetic and intellectual demand of wealthy collectors.

61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.name: Qur’anic illumination.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.description:
The right-hand page has the illumination, which is framed inside a gilt rectangle. The central decoration has two concave diamond shapes with a gilt background marked with brown lines framing stylised multi-lobed fleurons. The decoration is surrounded on each side by six triangles containing similar floral motifs. The whole illumination is separated by strips on a white background dotted with brown markings and divided by gilt segments.  
The left-hand page contains black *kufic* script. Vowels are marked by red dots and the *hamza* is shown with a green dot, as in the Abi al-Aswad system. The end of the verse is indicated by a triangle of three gilt dots. The end of the fifth verse is marked by a gilt medallion.  
The title of the *sura*, with the number of its verses, is indicated on the same line by a gilt *kufic* inscription with brown edges which terminates in a palm-leaf motif pointing towards the left-hand margin.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.short_description:
The illumination, in a gold rectangular frame on the right-hand page, has two concave lozenges in its centre, gilded at the bottom and peppered with brown lines.  
The left-hand page is written in black *kufic* script with the title of the *sura* and the number of verses given in golden *kufic* script.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.initial_owner: The Qur’an was part of a legacy (*habus*) left to the Great Mosque of Kairouan by Fadhl Mawlat Abi Ayub.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.method_for_datation: The colophon of the Qur'an includes the Act of Mortmain (*Tahbis*) dated 295 / 907.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.method_for_provenance: This Qur'an was copied and left to the Great Mosque of Kairouan by a woman who appears to be Kairouanese. It was probably copied in Kairouan itself which was a great centre of book production at the time.
61e3f563-8d0b-554f-837e-efc244795bf1.obtention: After the abolition of the *habus* foundation in Tunisia, the National Library obtained this Qur'an in 1967. In 1983 it went back to Kairouan, to the Centre of the Islamic Arts and Civilisation of Raqqada. It has been displayed at the Raqqada Museum of Islamic Art since 1986.

620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.name: Qur’an.
620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.description:
Two books of this multi-volume Qur'an, of which pages 100 and 101 of book II are shown here, are the only ones kept in the Rabat National Library. On almost square pages, they are both in Maghrebi *kufic* script in brown ink on parchment. Although in the same style, the calligraphy in the two volumes is not the same, suggesting the work of two copyists. However, judging from the thickness of the lines, the roundness in the angles of the letters and the depth of the curves, the two styles belong to the same period and to the same Qur'an. *Kufic* script in the West started to differ from the oriental style in the second half of the AH 3rd / AD 9th century, evolving towards a style known as Maghrebi, which reached maturity two centuries later. This type of writing, which continued to obey Abu al-Aswad's archaic system of vocalisation, has no diacritical marks. Only the short vowels are represented (*fatha*, the letter A ; *damma*, the letter O, red dots over the line), *kasra* (the letter I, red dot under the line), and *shedda* (indicating the duplication of the letter) which today is written like a lower case *w*. The yellow and green round dots denote the vocal attack.  
In this Qur'an, the titles of the suras lack any specific decoration. Only small golden rosettes framed by little dots, alternately blue and red, mark the separation between the verses, whereas the big rosettes, delicately adorned, embellish the verses in groups of ten. The written forms found in this specimen could link it to Zirid Qur'ans. Some very regular small punched holes in the upper margin of every page, where the word *habus* appears, prove that this book was brought as a pious offering to a shrine, probably in Fez.
620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.short_description: This Qur'an transcribed on parchment was offered as a pious gift to a shrine. The square format and the archaic *kufic* script with its rounded angles are characteristic of the Maghrebi calligraphy of the period. The red dots and golden rosettes mark the vowels and the separation of the verses.
620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.method_for_datation: Format and stylistic analysis of the script: archaic *kufic* style, codified for the system of vocalisation devised by Abu al-Aswad ad Du'ali (68 / 688) and adopted in the Muslim world from the 2nd–3rd / 8th–9th centuries. The calligraphy in these two volumes of the Qur'an is similar to the Western variant, known as Maghrebi.
620147b9-073c-55b0-9874-1ee32624af18.method_for_provenance: This Qur'an is thought to be from Fez, as the town was the Idrisid capital and home of the Qarawiyyin university.

6204d094-907f-5ef3-b378-936a43e07247.name: An Entertainment Scene (The third day of entertainment) from *Surname-i Vehbi*
6204d094-907f-5ef3-b378-936a43e07247.short_description: These images show events that took place on the Golden Horn on the evening of the third day. In them, we see the sultan seated in a tent on the Arsenal Palace quay surrounded by attendants. Two rafts are floating by. The one at the right, of which we can only see a part but appears to be a platform mounted on a pair of caiques, was donated by Yeğen Mehmed Pasha, Superintendent of the Customs Office. The figures of two rams suspended on gears and pulleys from the roof butt one another. This is following a real raft on which are set two gigantic dummies that face backwards and are dressed in Persian garb. At the front of the raft is a huge wheel of fireworks that one of the pyrotechnicists is causing to revolve. Its supporting frame is surmounted by a fire-spewing bird and rockets hurtle this way and that.

647040db-954c-553c-b7b9-c7c2901d4516.name: Album of calligraphies including poetry and prophetic traditions (*hadith*)
647040db-954c-553c-b7b9-c7c2901d4516.short_description: This album contains samples written by one of the most celebrated Turkish calligraphers, Shaikh Hamdullah (d. 1519), who developed the *naskhi* and *thuluth* styles from masters of the past to suit Ottoman taste. These pages, which show control, exactitude, and gentle flow, but also exaggeration of some letters to create a lively rhythmic pattern, demonstrate the calligrapher’s mature phase. The text comes from the hadith, the compilation of the Prophet Muhammad's words and deeds that is an important source for moral and legal guidance in the Islamic tradition. On each page, several lines of a small script (*naskhi*) are framed by one or two lines in a larger script (*thuluth* or *muhaqqaq*) and then pasted onto sheets of marbleized paper, which developed in Turkey and came to be much favored for calligraphic works.

649d4fc6-efad-5c54-848f-c9739373ad0f.name: *The Elephant Clock*, folio from a *Book of the Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices* by al-Jazari
649d4fc6-efad-5c54-848f-c9739373ad0f.short_description: This folio comes from a treatise on fantastic devices invented by the author Isma‘il al-Jazari. His elephant clock was especially intricate: every half hour, the bird on the dome whistled, the man below dropped a ball into the dragon’s mouth, and the driver hit the elephant with his goad. This automaton is reminiscent of the elaborate clocks found on medieval town halls in Europe, which made the passage of time more entertaining through the performance of the moving figures. The folio is a rare survival from Syria, where few such manuscripts from this date are known.

66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.name: *Zubdat al-Tawarikh* (‘Cream of Histories’).
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.description:
The work is written in Turkish with large *naskhi* script in black ink on 90 leaves of delicate finished (*aharlı*) paper. Within are 55 miniatures depicting subjects in the text, some of them one to a page and some two. On pages 1b–2a two round medallions carry an inscription stating the work's subject and saying that it was prepared for the Treasury of Sultan Murad III (r. AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95). The text is written 37 lines to a page; the titles and chapter headings are gilded. Their illumination features floral compositions with arabesques (*rumi*) and Chinese-inspired motifs (*hatayi*-style), while that of the first two pages' medallions includes large floral motifs (*halkar*\-style).  
  
The work's dark-green cover is lacquered using a technique known as *Edirnekari*. The outer covers are richly decorated with gold and silver in floral compositions, while the inner covers feature medallions, pendants and corner-pieces. The binding is not original.  
  
The work, which was written by the court panegyrist (*Şehnameci*) Sayyid Loqman Aşuri, consists of two main sections. The first begins with the universe and the signs of the zodiac and continues with stories taken from the Torah, the New Testament, and the Qur'an which tell of the lives of prophets and those who rendered service to the faith. These are illustrated with paintings. The first part ends with genealogical trees of the Prophet Muhammad, the Four Orthodox Caliphs, and the sultans and high officials of Muslim dynasties such as the Umayyads, the 'Abbasids, the early Islamic period, the Ghaznawids, the Ilkhanids, the Seljuqs and the Timurids. The second part opens with Sultan Osman, the founder of the Ottoman dynasty, and goes up to Sultan Murad III, with 12 portraits of Ottoman sultans. It ends with descriptions of the political events of these sultans' reigns.  
  
This work was made for the Treasury of Sultan Murad III, and the quality of its paintings, its binding and its calligraphy make it one of the greatest works of Ottoman art created for a sultan.
66dee6a2-095c-5e95-9ab7-3051179223bf.short_description: This manuscript includes stories of the prophets, the birth of Islam and histories of Muslim states. It was written on the order of Sultan Murad III by the historian Sayyid Lokman and illuminated by famous *naqqash* (painters) Molla Kasım and Ustad Osman. It is a unique work of Ottoman art.

66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.name: *Divan-ı* Ali Şir Nevai (Social Gathering for Entertainment)
66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.description:
This copy of Ali Şîr Nevâî's *Divan*, a collection of poems written under his pseudonym, Fânî, is dated Hegira 943 / AD 1536–1537, and is signed by Mir Ali al-Bukhârî. It is written in Chagatai Turkish in *Nastaliq* calligraphy in two columns on papers of various colours with different patterns and *zerefşan* (gold leaf).  
On page 1a is a text written in a circular medallion with superscript text. This states that the work was prepared for Abdülazîz Khan, b. Ubeydullah Khan, one of the rulers of the Shaybânî Dynasty, an Islamic dynasty that ruled in Mâverâünnehir, Khârezm and Khorasan. At the top of the same page is the seal of Sultan Mahmud I's foundation, and below it is the seal of Derviş Mustafa Efendi, inspector of Evkaf. On the following facing pages is a scene of entertainment in the countryside. The title page is decorated with floral and geometric motifs. There are a total of eight miniatures in the work.  
The binding comprises two covers, the outer of which is leather over cardboard. It is decorated with Chinese clouds and various floral motifs on a gilt ground. The inner cover is made of brown leather, and the backgrounds of borders, corners, and edges of panels are navy blue. These sections with navy blue grounds are decorated with floral motifs obtained by the *kat’ı* (paper cutting) technique.

66ef3821-0608-5a20-9446-662a31c4e610.obtention: The item was brought to the Museum from the Mahmud I Library on 13 April 1914.

6727ef2a-3a08-5d1f-a254-abd5bdf97f5f.name:
Isfandiyar’s second exploit: he kills two lions  
Folio from a dispersed copy of Firdausi’s *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings)
6727ef2a-3a08-5d1f-a254-abd5bdf97f5f.short_description: Recounting the story of Iran from mythical times through to the arrival of the Muslim Arabs in the mid-7th century AD, the epic poem the *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings) was originally completed in 1010 by the poet Firdausi. These dramatic scenes centering on Isfandiyar, son of King Gushtasp, were included in a 1341 Shahnameh that is now dispersed. The story of Isfandiyar’s exploits recalls the seven trials that the great hero Rustam underwent in his quest to liberate King Kay Kavus from captivity in a much earlier Shahnameh story. Isfandiyar endured his labours en route to rescuing his two sisters, who were captured during the ongoing war between Iran and Turan. Isfandiyar decided to take the shortest but most dangerous route to the Brazen Hold, the Turanian fortress made of brass where his sisters were imprisoned.

672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.name: Page from a Qur’an.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.description:
The Fatiha *sura* ('the Opening', verses 1 and 2), taken from a Qur'an copied on parchment.  
The writing combines the *kufic, naskhi* and the *rayhani* styles. Its identity has still not been well established. The laying out of the cursive script is more rectangular than curved.  
Vowel-points are absent from this writing, but, in keeping with the system developed by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, there is an abundance of orthographic signs. Vowels are marked in red, *sukun* and *shadda* in blue and *hamza* and *maddah* in brilliant green.  
Standing out on this page is a strip containing the title and number of verses in the following *sura*, written in gold.  
The title is inscribed in a series of superimposed frames in which geometric decoration alternates with floral decoration using the multi-lobed fleuron. Some strips are engraved in gold and all the surrounds are brown. A palm-leaf motif made up of floral arabesques projects towards the edge of the page.  
At the top of the page in the right-hand margin there is a geometrically decorated gold and brown lozenge; the corners each have a crown in the same colour and the sides have blue and brown circles on the outer edge.  
The central area contains gilded *kufic* script indicating the number of the verses.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.short_description: This page is from a Qur'an copied on vellum. Bands of geometric decoration with the name of the *sura* and the number of verses it contains, in gold, are particularly distinctive. The colophon of the Qur'an mentions the deed of gift by the governess of Prince Badis to the Great Mosque of Kairouan.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.initial_owner: Fatima al-Hadinah, governess to the Zirid prince, Badis.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.dimensions: Length 45.5 cm, width 31 cm; 5 lines, 1 folio.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.method_for_datation: The deed of gift clearly mentions that the legacy took place in 410 / 1020.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.method_for_provenance: This Qur'an was copied, illuminated and bound by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Warraq for Fatima al-Hadinah, the governess of the Zirid prince, Badis. The work was supervised and financed by Durah al-Katibah – 'Durah the lady-scribe', the governess's secretary. The colophon of the Qur'an mentions the deed of gift by Badis's governess to the Great Mosque of Kairouan. The deed is authorised by the *qadi* (judge) of Kairouan, Abdullah ibn Hashim.
672e5d81-e294-5bdc-9691-e88fb689a760.obtention: After the abolition of the *habus* foundation in Tunisia, this Qur'an was obtained by the Bardo Museum. In 1986 it was transferred to the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada where it is currently on display.

67ae5352-aaad-57a1-9050-4df90cfc07e6.name: *Suz u gudaz* (‘Burning and Melting’)
67ae5352-aaad-57a1-9050-4df90cfc07e6.short_description: *Suz u gudaz* (‘Burning and Melting’) is a romance, an allegorical poem that tells of the soul’s yearning for God through the story of a Hindu woman who, following the custom known as *sati*, ended her life on her husband’s funeral pyre. The poet Muhammad Riza, known as Naw‘i (d.1619), was born in Khabushan in north-eastern Iran, but later travelled to India where he composed the poem for Prince Daniyal, son of the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605). The three paintings shown here depict the worship of fire, the young man telling his father of his beloved, and the two lovers seated in a garden with an attendant standing nearby.

681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.name: Qazwini, Zakariya Ibn-Muhammad al-, Tuhfatu i-Gharaʾib (ʿAjaʾibu i-Mahluqat wa Gharaʾibu i-Mawjudat) (The Gift of Oddities)
681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.short_description: This manuscript is a Persian copy of Zakariya Ibn-Muhammad al-Qazwini’s (1203-1283) Arabic original “Tuhfatu i-Gharaʾib” (“The Gift of Oddities”) calligraphed by the scribe Pir Husain al-Katib. This copy can be localised in Shiraz and was inspired by the Herati style however it also reflects Turkmen and Safavid styles as well. The date 1492 is mentioned in the colophon and soon after its production, it is likely that it came into the collection of Shah Tahmasp (1514-1576), whose seal can be found within. The manuscript has richly embellished double opening pages situated within a decorative blue and gold colour scheme interspersed with floral scrolls and colourful buds and flowers. There are 204 illustrations scattered across various pages of the manuscript showing constellations, zodiacal signs, celestial symbols, animals, and fantastical creatures, among other depictions. These paintings mostly occupy a small section of the text area, and often protrude into the empty margins that surround the written text. There are occasional colour abrasions in the illustrations, as well as some miniatures having been painted over in the early Safavid period, but they are mostly well-preserved.
681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.dimensions: 240 x 170mm (text area 145 x 95mm). ff. I, I*, 310.
681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.method_for_provenance: Seal of Tahmasp I. (1514–1576). This object is presumably from the collection of Jakob von Wallenburg (d. 1806). It was also part of the collection of Graf Wenceslaus von Rzewuski (d. 1831), after which it entered the collection of Joseph Freiherr von Hammer-Purgstall (d. 1856; his seal is on f. 310b).
681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.obtention: Entered the Austrian National Library in 1842.

681543eb-7d4b-5d8f-91c4-bdb708f84dc9.binding_desc: The dark brown leather binding with a renewed green flap was likely produced in early 16th-century Tabriz, and restored in 1921 in Vienna. The front and back cover include a cut-out medallion with corner pieces created as recessed leather inlays with gold relief stamping. From a central rosette, a flower tendril extends upwards and downwards in an S-shape. Within, four symmetrically arranged cranes or herons are depicted in mid-flight. The extensions directly above and below attached to the central medallion include a seated hare. The spine, which has been renewed, has three cartouches with gold-stamped leather inlay, showing floral tendrils ending in animal heads. The leather doublures also show a cut-out medallion design containing delicate arabesque leather filigree on a blue ground, with golden contour lines.

68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.name: *Siyer-i Nebi* (‘Biography of the Prophet’).
68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.description:
The work is written in Turkish on delicate finished (*aharlı*) paper using 13 lines per page of large *naskhi* script. The text is written within gilded margins in black ink; proper names are written in red ink. The areas between the lines of text are filled with gilding whose edges are traced in black. The six-volume *Siyer-i Nebi* or 'Biography of the Prophet' tells of the life of the Prophet Muhammad and of the history of Islam up until his death. The volume in the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts is a copy of the fourth volume and has 545 folios. A total of 193 miniatures depict the subjects within. The first page, an illuminated title page, is decorated with gilding. On those pages with miniatures, the painting is situated between the top and bottom two lines of text. The volume's brown leather binding is adorned with an oval medallion with palmette pendants and corner-pieces.  
  
The fourth volume begins with the birth of the Prophet's daughter, Fatima, and goes on to describe her marriage to 'Ali; the miracles of Muhammad; the love of Talha and Gamza; tales of heroic Muslim women; the preparation for the battle of Badr and the battle itself; Muhammad's wounding at the battle of Uhud; the death of the Prophet's uncle Hamza; the distribution of the spoils of war; the story of Ka'b and his daughter; and the killing of the Muslims' enemy, Sufyan ibn Khalid.  
  
*Siyer-i Nebi* was prepared in six volumes by the palace atelier at the behest of Sultan Murad III in the AH 10th / AD 16th century. Today one volume is lost, while the others are dispersed in libraries around the world. The manuscript in the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts is a copy (made in the AH 11th- / AD 17th-century) of a manuscript of the fourth volume of *Siyer-i Nebi* in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin, (T. 419). The miniatures are stylistically typical of the period.
68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.short_description: This AH 11th- / AD 17th-century copy of *Siyer-i Nebi*, literally 'Life of the Prophet', has an important place in Ottoman art not only because of subject but also because of its binding, the figurative style of its miniatures, and its architectural compositions.

68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.method_for_datation: The style of the miniatures is characteristic of the 11th / 17th century.
68ecd47c-38f6-579b-9162-d8283100397d.method_for_provenance: Manuscripts of this quality and cost can only have been made in the palace atelier.

690ddb14-8419-58b9-8cc0-666d98a20849.name: Abu Mansur Muwaffaq ibn 'Ali al-Harawi, *Kitab al-Abniya 'an haqa'iq ad-adwiya* ('The Book of Fundamentals on the True Nature of Remedies')
690ddb14-8419-58b9-8cc0-666d98a20849.short_description: This is the oldest known surviving Islamic manuscript in the Persian language. It is a copy of the 10th-century writer Abu Mansur Muwaffaq ibn 'Ali al-Harawi’s so-called *Kitab al-Abniya 'an haqa'iq ad-adwiya* (‘The Book of Fundamentals on the True Nature of Remedies’), the content of which he attributes to the Samanid writer Mansur b. Nuh around 350-365 AH / 961-976 AD. According to the colophon, this manuscript was written in monumental calligraphic angular (*kufic*) script by 'Ali b. Ahmad al-Asadi at-Tusi Ash-Shatr in 447 AH / 1055-56 AD, possibly in Nakhchivan, Azerbaijan. This writer was also a poet who wrote the heroic epic entitled *Garshaspnama*, which was based on the famous ‘Book of Kings’ (*Shahnama*). The copy is dedicated to an *ar-ra'is al-jalil al-amjad* Abu'l-Qasim. In the margins, Turkish glosses from a later time reveal the manuscript’s stay in Turkey after which it can be traced to the inventory of the Austrian National Library in 1811.

69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.name: *Noah’s Ark*
69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.short_description:
Timur’s son Shah Rukh (r. AH 808-851 / AD 1405-1447) ordered the historian Hafiz-i Abru to write a continuation of Rashid al-Din’s famous history of the world, Jami al-tawarikh. Like the Il-Khanids, the Timurids were concerned with legitimizing their right to rule, and Hafiz-i Abru’s “A Collection of Histories” covers a period that included the time of Shah Rukh himself.  
  
The style of the manuscript’s miniatures is slightly old-fashioned compared with the otherwise refined Timurid painting, but the scene on the stormy sea is quite dramatic, with the fluttering sail, the ark breaking out of the picture frame and the swollen bodies. The animals that are to populate the earth are rendered both humorously and fairly realistically.

6a2ad1b6-4e61-5b64-aa4c-e23e31a8188c.name: *Sübhatü'l Ebrar* by Molla Camii
6a2ad1b6-4e61-5b64-aa4c-e23e31a8188c.description:
Molla Camii was a poet and scientist of the Naqshbandi order who was born and raised in Samarkand during the Timuri period (1414–1492). He was a highly renowned figure during his lifetime, and was frequently invited by the Ottoman sultans.  
In this miniature Prophet Abraham and a fire-worshipping priest are depicted. Prophet Abraham informs the pagan priest that he can invite him to his table only if the priest accepts Islam. The elderly priest, declaring that he would not alter his beliefs for a mere morsel of bread, rises from the table and departs. At this point, a voice from the heavens is heard saying it is unjust to compel an elderly man to leave the table hungry, regardless of his beliefs. Prophet Abraham then realises his error and invites the priest back to the table. The priest, after being invited a subsequent time, becomes a believer upon being told what had happened.  
In the miniature, Prophet Abraham's head is haloed and his face is veiled. He points to the food, indicating that the priest should join him.
materials: finished *(aharlı)* paper, ink, leather binding

6a7f88ad-e38f-5e65-b83b-d07699dcfcd7.name: *Zubdat al-Tawarikh* (‘Cream of Histories’)
6a7f88ad-e38f-5e65-b83b-d07699dcfcd7.short_description: Muslims consider the Qur’an the third and final portion of God’s revelation to mankind: it completes, but does not supplant, God’s earlier revelations to the Jews and Christians. The prophets of the Old and New Testaments are therefore also prophets in Islam. This manuscript is a history of the world beginning with Adam and ending with the Ottoman sultans of the sixteenth century. It includes depictions of various prophets common to all three religions (such as Abraham and Ishmael), as well as specifically Islamic prophets (such as Alexander and Khizr). The manuscript ends with a depiction of Sultan Murad III (r. AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95), during whose reign the manuscript was produced. Each prophet or sultan is identified by an inscription.
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination; lacquer; Edirnekari technique; gilding; ink; paper; painting; watercolour; zodiac
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

6cac4f71-4c6d-5af5-91b7-33d7f396babe.name: *Iyar-i Danish* (‘Touchstone of Wisdom’)
6cac4f71-4c6d-5af5-91b7-33d7f396babe.short_description: The text of *Iyar-i danish* (‘Touchstone of Wisdom’) derives from the collection of Sanskrit animal fables known as Panchatantra and thought to have been compiled sometime before AD 500. Since then, several versions of the fables have appeared, in ancient Pahlavi, Persian and Arabic. The version known as *Iyar-i danish* was compiled at the Mughal court for the emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605). The fables are part of the genre of literature known as ‘mirrors for princes’, consisting of stories intended to instruct rulers in the art of statecraft. Each chapter of the text consists of a frame story dealing with a specific moral. The characters of the frame story then each tell their own stories of behaviour exemplifying the moral in question.
keywords: fables; stories; literature; manuscript; animal; Kalila wa dimna; lion; fox; miniature painting; illustration; education
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.name: Al-Hariri, *Maqamat* ('Assemblies')
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.short_description: The Arab poet Al-Hariri of Basra, or Abu Muhammad al-Qasim ibn Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Uthman al-Hariri (d. 516 AH / 1122 AD), wrote the *Maqamat al-Hariri* (‘Assemblies of Hariri), which is a collection of fifty stories written in the *Maqama* style of rhymed prose with intervals of poetry. Al-Hariri also extensively utilises Arabic idioms and proverbs. While this style of writing was developed a century earlier, Al-Hariri elevated this genre into a major literary form through this work. In his *Maqamat*, the anecdotes are told by the roguish wanderer and eloquent trickster Abu Zayd to the narrator, al-Harith b. Hammam al-Basri. This copy was written in calligraphic large Mamluk *naskh* script by Abu'l-Fada'il b. Abi Ishaq in 734 AH / 1334 AD. The quality of the manuscript, its courtly title page, and large format suggest that it was created in Cairo, then capital of the Mamluk Sultanate and Caliphate. The sultan who possibly commissioned the manuscript and who may be the one depicted on the dedicatory title page is An-Nasir Muhammad b. Qala'un, who was in power for the third time from 709 AH / 1309-10 AD to 741 AH / 1340-41 AD. The manuscript includes seventy paintings, which must have been completed by a group of artists or a workshop. It is likely that multiple pages are no longer extant. The images that are preserved reflect a Mamluk style of painting, including bright colours on a golden background, more monumentalised scenes, and a reduction to essential elements in expression and composition, especially when compared to the Persian-Seljuk style of Baghdad and Mosul book-painting. The figures’ facial features follow the Turkish-Mongolian ideal of beauty that emerged under the Seljuks in Persia. The essential principle of composition throughout the manuscript is the juxtaposition of individual figures with figural groups, whereby means of deliberate contrast or symmetry are employed. These compositions underline the textual structure of the stories. The manuscript probably entered the Austrian National Library between 1820 and 1840.
6cd1576c-84dc-565e-8f5b-d3d3ed636ea8.dimensions: 373 x 260 mm (c. 260 x 160mm), ff. II, II*, 195 folios.

6e13aca8-8a19-574f-8378-12aea190e022.name: File 3142/1903 'Hedjaz Railway'
6e13aca8-8a19-574f-8378-12aea190e022.description:
This volume contains copies of correspondence between British officials regarding the construction of the Hijaz Railway. The correspondence discusses a number of different aspects of the railway including its route, the progress of its construction and donations made towards its construction by members of the Muslim community in India.  
  
A limited amount of the correspondence in the volume is in French, including a copy of a letter sent by Paul Cambon, the French Ambassador in London, to Sir Edward Grey, the Foreign Secretary (folio 15).  
  
The volume contains a number of reports and related information about the railway. Of particular interest are the following:  
  
A report on the Hijaz Railway by Major Francis Richard Maunsell, dated July 1907 (ff 56-69)  
A memorandum respecting German influence on the Hijaz Railway by George Ambrose Lloyd, 1906 (ff 95-96)  
A list of the principal stations on the Hijaz Railway with approximate distances between Damascus and each station (f 100)  
A map of the Hijaz Railway with list of stations (f 106)  
A report by Mr Teofani Loiso, Vice-Consul at Mersina, based on information provided to him by his son who was employed as an engineer on the railway (ff 105-107)  
A report by Herr Otto von Kapp Kohlstein, a German engineer who inspected the Haifa-Damascus branch of the route and worked on the construction of the Damascus-Maan branch (ff 107-109).  
In addition, the volume contains cuttings (and translations) of press articles related to several aspects of the railway and its construction. Also included are two maps. The Turkish (Ottoman) language material consists of the second of these two maps.  
  
The volume includes a divider which gives the year that the subject file was opened, the subject heading, and a list of correspondence references contained in it arranged by year. This divider is placed at the front of the volume.

6eafd8d2-5a3d-5f7f-b16f-0753d6373196.name: Possibly Yusuf b. 'Abdüllatif, *Sübhet al-Akhbar* (The Rosary of World History, Genealogy of Ottoman Personalities)
6eafd8d2-5a3d-5f7f-b16f-0753d6373196.short_description: The elaborate genealogy or chain book, titled *Sübhet al-Akhbar* (‘The Rosary of World History’) was likely written by Yusuf b. 'Abdüllatif (died 1545), a court genealogist under Suleyman the Magnificent in Istanbul, around 1094 AH / 1683 AD. Since the historical information in the text dates back to 1678, the manuscript itself must have been created shortly after this period, before the deposition and death of Qara Mustafa Pasha, which occurred at the end of 1683. The text later became part of the library of Prince Eugene of Savoy in 1716 and was ultimately acquired by the Austrian National Library in 1727. Family trees and their graphical representation in the form of linked circular medallions – hence also the classification as a *Silsile-name* – have been an old tradition in Islam since the early 14th century. The literary form of such genealogies referring to ancestors, however, originated under Suleyman the Magnificent in the 16th century. Starting with Adam and Eve, these manuscripts progress from the great biblical prophets and legendary rulers of Iran to the most distinguished Arabic, Mongol, Persian, and Turkish dynasties, and conclude with the contemporaneous rulers of the Ottoman Empire. These types of genealogies were often conceived as scrolls, which are even reflected in book form within this manuscript, as the connecting lines extend downwards in a vertical manner. These family trees are of great cultural and art-historical interest as large quantities of them are in existence, and reveal the manifold artistic source materials that even draw on European models. Moreover, their political objective to legitimise the Ottoman rule based on previous history reveals the self-representation of Ottomans as well as their visual evaluation of specific ancestral figures. As these genealogies are traced back to pagan or biblical times, the names of saints become part of a dynastic claim of legitimacy and historical awareness. From fol. 4b onwards, genealogical trees are depicted in a vertical manner, including inscribed or figuratively painted medallions of various sizes connected by red and blue lines. It is possible that the circular shape of the portraits was derived from ancient to medieval coins and medals with the ruler's portraits. These 102 paintings throughout the text are accompanied by the figures’ names in red script. Moreover, radiating, oblique or upside-down blocks of text – usually a short vita of the person – and inscriptions in smaller black script are added around them. The background is filled with delicate gold floral vine designs. According to the signature on the final painting, they were made by the painter Hüseyin al-Istanbuli. They are executed in a particularly high quality, utilise rich colours, and are modelled delicately. Gold and silver are lavishly used; a hierarchical difference is established by utilising a golden background for the depiction of saints while ruler figures are set within a different context of a landscape. The portraits of the Ottoman sultans follow a typification that had developed since the 16th century and is believed to have been so wide-spread that historically educated people could recognise the rulers based on their most distinctive facial features, their hairstyle, their garments, and their attributes. A comparable yet less elaborate manuscript in Ankara (Vakıflar Genel Müdürlüğü, manuscript K-4) was copied in the same workshop and illuminated by the same painter, with the signature also found on the last portrait of the sultan, with a date of 1094 AH / 1683 AD. The Ottoman court style of this period is characterised by a mixture of European and Ottoman artistic traditions with a detailed realism, plastic modelling, cubic perspective motifs, richness of ornamental elements, and *horror vacui*, contrasted with a bright polychromy, and two-dimensional ornamental compositions.

6f08705f-4fcd-53b3-897e-4ec99dd97489.name: *Wonders of Creation*
6f08705f-4fcd-53b3-897e-4ec99dd97489.short_description: Zakariya Qazwini’s extremely popular *‘Aja’ib al-mukhluqat* (‘Wonders of Creation’) was compiled in AD 1270. The text describes various real and imagined marvels of the universe, exploring the fields of geography, astronomy, astrology and natural history. His text, originally written in Arabic, was later translated into both Persian and Turkish. Most copies are heavily illustrated. This particular copy includes more than 500 illustrations, including depictions of a peacock, the monkeys and other fauna of the island of Java, the *Shadadar*, a unicorn with a musical horn and an anatomical diagram of a pregnant woman. The manuscript opens with a fine illuminated double-page frontispiece.
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination; science; anatomy; astrology; astronomy; imaginary animal
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

6fd22e74-7aec-530f-aa12-acba198db8f8.name: *Siyar-i Nabi* (‘Life of the Prophet’)
6fd22e74-7aec-530f-aa12-acba198db8f8.short_description: In Cairo, in the late fourteenth-century, al-Darir wrote a *siyar-i nabi* (life of the prophet). Earlier such texts had been written, but al-Darir’s was the first to be written in Turkish, the language of the ruling Mamluk dynasty of Egypt. Some two hundred years later, in Istanbul, the Ottoman sultan Murad III (r. AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95), commissioned a six-volume copy of al-Darir’s text. These illustrations are from the fourth volume of that manuscript, the volume dealing with the battles of Badr (AD 624) and Uhud (AD 625). The illustrations are the work of several individuals and are generally executed in a simple and direct style.
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination; tent; camel
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

706091ba-1c94-588c-882c-871fe5fdaca3.name: Miniature 'Mi'raj (the Miraculous Ascension) of Prophet Muhammad'
706091ba-1c94-588c-882c-871fe5fdaca3.short_description: Mi'raj is the scene of the Ascension of the Great Prophet Muhammad to Heaven to the throne of Allah. The iconography of the scene has become established in the Iranian painting tradition since the late AD 15th century. The composition of Mi'raj, together with the poetic dedication of God and His Prophet, traditionally opened manuscripts of historical, biographical and poetic works of classical Persian literature. In the centre of the scene we see Prophet Muhammad riding the fantastic animal Boraq, a mare with a woman’s head. Muhammad is traditionally depicted with a large flaming halo around his head. His face is covered by a veil, probably added to the picture later. In front of the Prophet, we see the Archangel Jabriel showing the way. Above the Archangel there is a lion, the heavenly personification of Ali, the first righteous Imam of the Shiites. Angels with gifts fly around the Prophet. Between the figures against the blue sky, golden "Chinese" clouds abound. The miniature subject combines two important Islamic legends. The Qur'anic Al-Isra (Night Journey, Surah 17) recounts the Prophet's magical night flight from Mecca to Jerusalem. The Al-Mi'raj (Staircase), narrated in hadiths, is the story of Muhammad's miraculous ascent to Heaven to the throne of God.
706091ba-1c94-588c-882c-871fe5fdaca3.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by V. Krachkovskaya (publication, 1926, origin and date).
706091ba-1c94-588c-882c-871fe5fdaca3.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927): the Khanenkos' collection.

70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.name: Abu Yahya Zakariyya' ibn Muhammad al-Qazwini, *'Aga'ib al-makhluqat wa-ghara'ib al-maujudat* ('The Wonders of Creation and the Marvels of Creation')
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.short_description: Abu Zakariyya' ibn Muhammad al-Qazwini (600-682 AH / 1203-1283 AD) wrote the famous treatise ‘The Wonders of Creatures and the Marvels of Creation’ (*'Aja'ib al-Makhluqat wa Ghara'ib al-Mawjudat*). According to the colophon, this copy was written in 1174 AH / 1761 AD by al- Hajji 'Ali, one of the freedmen of 'Abdalhaiy Auda Pasha and likely created in Ottoman-dynasty Cairo, Egypt. As the owners’ stamp indicates, the manuscript later belonged to Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall, and was acquired by the Austrian National Library in 1842. In the early 19th century, the manuscript and binding were probably supplemented and restored, yet their original look has been preserved. Its contemporaneous leather binding exhibits Ottoman-style decoration, while its 455 paintings of various sizes and shapes seen throughout the manuscript. They seem to have been created to mimic medieval models of painting, which were not fully understood, or perhaps just poorly preserved. Interestingly, the images are in stark contrast with the neat Egyptian writing style in *naskh* script. The flat painting style throughout includes raw outlines and bright colours, all of which give the paintings a dramatic and, at times, comic expression that may be comparable to later Coptic painting.
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.method_for_provenance: On fol. 312b, an owner's stamp by Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall dated to 1223 AH / 1808 AD is visible.
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.obtention: Acquired  in 1842 from Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall.
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.bibliography: Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften II. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 5, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1992: 111-116.
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.binding_desc: The brown leather binding features gilt inlays of thin light-brown leather, which are stamped with floral motifs in the Ottoman style. The binding consists of a flap that has a recessed pointed medallion with pendants at its centre. Hand-painted cord or interlace motifs are visible on the overall frame, and immediately inside this frame are small, stamped floral details. The binding was likely produced in 18th-century Cairo, Egypt.

71082c7e-eac1-551e-a256-81448d398bf5.name: *Jihannuma* (View of the world)
71082c7e-eac1-551e-a256-81448d398bf5.short_description:
Katip Celebi went down in history as a gifted polymath. Born as Mustafa ibn 'Abd Allah in Istanbul in 1017 AH / 1609 AD, he started his studies in Arabic calligraphy and grammar when he was a mere six years old. He was said to be an exceptional writer, which later on earned him the name Katip Celebi, literally translating to "Learned Scribe". His passion for learning made him interested in various fields of study including lexicology, logic, rhetoric, mathematics, medicine, geography, astronomy, genealogy, history and chronicling. In addition to writing books and treatises in Turkish, Arabic and Persian, Katip Celebi also translated texts from French and Latin.  
This particular manuscript is a rarity for two main reasons, one that it is the first edition of Katip Celebi's famous geographical book *Jihannuma*, and the second being that it contains additional notes for the planned second edition. The presence of these reconsiderations has earnt the manuscript another name, the "Viennese Concept", as it clearly documents Katip Celebi's process of revising his own work and assembling a second edition of the *Jihannuma*. Finally, it is important to note that parts of the text were written and annotated by the Learned Scribe himself.
71082c7e-eac1-551e-a256-81448d398bf5.method_for_provenance: On fol. 45a there is "ex bibliotheca orientali Wenceslai Comitis Rzewuski" written in ink.

718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.name: Page from a Qur’an.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.description: Al-Takathur *sura* ('The Rivalry', 102: 8) and al-Asr *sura* ('The Time', 103: 1). This page is taken from a Qur'an written in black *kufic* script. The vowels are marked with red diacritic dots and the *hamza* and *shadda* are indicated by green and yellow marks in the style of Abi al-Aswad, the Arab grammarian (d. AH 61 / AD 681). The verses are divided by a gilded green-centred rosette outlined in brown dots. The magnificent title of the *sura* is contained within an ornamental line of *kufic,* terminating in a palm-leaf motif which projects into the margin of the page. This palm-leaf is composed of stylised, gilded leaves and floral arabesques and is illuminated in blue and green with delicate touches of brown. These motifs are part of the decorative repertoire of Muslim illuminators and calligraphers from the AH 5th / AD 11th century.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.short_description: Written in black *kufic* script, this page contains two Qur'anic quotations (102: 8 and 103: 1). The division of verses is marked by a gold rosette with a green centre. All of the motifs belong to the decorative repertoire of Muslim illuminators and calligraphers after the AH 5th / AD 11th century.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.dates: Hegira, beginning of the second quarter of the 5th century / AD 9th century.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.method_for_datation: The Qur'an was given as a legacy (*habus*) by the Zirid prince, al-Mu'izz ibn Badis to the Great Mosque of Kairouan. The deed of gift dates from later than the break with Cairo, since it mentions the hatred of the prince for the Fatimids. According to historians this split began in 424 / 1033 and came to an end by 441 / 1050.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.method_for_provenance: This Qur'an was left to the Great Mosque by the reigning Zirid prince. Given that Kairouan was at that time a great centre of book production, it is highly likely that this example was copied and bound at Kairouan on locally tanned parchment.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.obtention: This Qur'an was obtained by the National Library in 1967 after the abolition of the *habus* foundation in Tunisia, and was transferred in 1983 to the Centre of Islamic Art and Civilisation at Raqqada. It has been displayed in the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada since 1986.

71964a69-73f1-55cb-a4b0-08031be5d50e.name: The peace treaty of Bucharest
71964a69-73f1-55cb-a4b0-08031be5d50e.short_description: The peace treaty that ended the Russo-Ottoman war of 1806-1812 was signed by the representatives of Russia and the Ottoman Empire in Bucharest, the capital of Wallachia, on the 28 May 1812. Both Wallachia and Moldavia had been occupied by Russia during the war. According to the third article of the peace treaty the Russian army had to liberate Wallachia and the Moldavian territory on the right side of the Prut River. The fourth article stipulated that Russia annexed the territory situated on the left side of the Prut, which became the new border between the Ottoman and the Russian Empires. The new area incorporated into the Russian Empire was given the name Bessarabia, which had in the past designated southern Moldavia.

71a4f299-e4d9-536c-9b45-df79ec3e4787.name: Single-volume Qur’an
71a4f299-e4d9-536c-9b45-df79ec3e4787.short_description:
The surviving left-hand folio of the double-page frontispiece (folio 1a) is designed as two overlapping circles in a braided frame, each containing part of the verse, letter and diacritical count. This derives from the illumination of early Qur’ans in oblong format and indicates that the transition to vertical format did not immediately bring a radical new layout. The manuscript ends with an illuminated double finispiece in which gold predominates. The pattern, here too, is based on overlapping circles.  
The text is copied in *naskhi*, with 20 lines to the page. *Sura* headings are in gold *kufic*, with a marginal gold palmette, which occasionally contains the name of the place where the *sura* was revealed. Individual verses are not marked, but groups of five verses are indicated by an oval and groups of ten by a circle.

71b58e2a-590f-5062-b329-444a2fef694c.name: "How Rustam Found a Spring"
71b58e2a-590f-5062-b329-444a2fef694c.alternate_name: Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi
71b58e2a-590f-5062-b329-444a2fef694c.description: The two miniatures 69.74.8 and 69.74.9 illustrate the first and second of Rustam's seven ordeals. The first depicts the frequently illustrated scene of Rustam's gallant horse Rakhsh killing a lion while the hero sleeps. The subject of the second miniature is, on the other hand, rarely depicted. Rustam and Rakhsh nearly die of heat and thirst in the desert before, with the help of divine providence, they find a spring. Rustam bathes and grooms his faithful steed by the water's edge, as seen here. The painter is very sympathetic to the closeness between the hero and his trustworthy Rakhsh.

72310d27-d35b-55e1-9286-57585ac375e7.name: *Silsila-nama* (‘Genealogy’)
72310d27-d35b-55e1-9286-57585ac375e7.short_description: These folios belong to one of a small group of manuscripts produced in the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, probably in Baghdad, for Ottoman Turkish patrons. These manuscripts are generally classed as genealogies (though they in fact do not function strictly as such) and are known by the name *silsila-nama*. They usually begin with an account of the Prophet Muhammad, followed by a history of the world from Adam to the reigning Ottoman sultan, and are illustrated with numerous small, medallion-like portraits of prophets and kings. Each individual depicted is identified by an inscription. The manuscript opens with an illuminated frontispiece.
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

7269ff1c-7668-58a5-a38d-e8ec83dace0c.name: *Zafarnāmah by Sharaf al-Din ʿAli Yazdi* (Timur's Return to Samarkand and the Festive Celebrations in the Garden of Bagh-ı Behesht)
7269ff1c-7668-58a5-a38d-e8ec83dace0c.description: *Zafarnāmah* is a significant historical text from the 15th century that describes Timur's leadership and achievements. Written by Şerafeddin Ali Yezdî (Hegira 858 / AD 1454), the work was commissioned by Timur's grandson, Ibrahim Sultan. As a historical source, *Zafarnāmah* is invaluable for its comprehensive information about Timur's life. The book was compiled using notes taken by Timur's royal scribes and secretaries, indicating that its contents were meticulously selected. Its most significant source is the biography of Timur, *Zafarnāmah*, written by Nizāmeddīn-i Sāmī in 1404. The primary distinction between Şerafeddin's *Zafarnāmah* and Sāmī’s earlier *Zafarnāmah* lies in the novel information presented in Şerafeddin's later version, and the more elaborate embellishments, including miniatures, in Sāmī’s earlier one.  The later work was inscribed by Hamdullah ibn al-Sheikh Murshid al-Kātib in Hegira 891 / AD 1486–1487, and is written in Persian with black ink in *taliq* calligraphy on fine paper. The work contains ten miniature scenes of rich workmanship, most of which depict Timur. The miniatures generally portray battles, council meetings and festivities that took place during the Timurid period. The first page contains the foundation seal of Hacı Mehmed Aga, the trustee of Teke Sancağı (Antalya region). The following page displays an illumination comprising geometric and floral motifs on blue and gilt backgrounds. The titles of the chapters and some of the prayers are written in gilt, red and blue ink.
7269ff1c-7668-58a5-a38d-e8ec83dace0c.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
7269ff1c-7668-58a5-a38d-e8ec83dace0c.obtention: The object was brought to the Museum from Antalya Müsellim Mosque on 31 March 1916.
materials: Finished (*aharli*) paper, ink, gilding, leather binding

72ae01c0-55bc-584b-8258-a81263d1edbd.name: *Hamzanama*: Emissaries bring news from the provinces of Khaybar and Chin to Anoshirvan
72ae01c0-55bc-584b-8258-a81263d1edbd.short_description: "Sergeants-at-arms hastened off to all parts of the realm and found two ancient bricks, one in Khaybar and one in Chin. They brought the two bricks to Anoshirvan and reported to the emperor of the seven climes. The king summoned the *khwaja* to his retinue and, in his presence, asked the sergeants why the two countries were in ruins. The sergeants reported that in Khaybar there was a guebre named Hisham who did everything he could by way of cruelty and injustice, while in Chin, although the Khaqan was very good, he had a son named Bahram Gur, who was extremely egotistical and unruly. The subjects of those two kingdoms were tormented by the injustice of those two, and on account of them the kingdoms were in ruins."

72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.name: *Surname-i Hümayun* (‘Book of the Imperial Circumcision Festival’).
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.description:
The *Surname-i Hümayun* ('Book of the Imperial Circumcision Festival') is a work dealing with the celebrations held for the circumcision festival of Prince Mehmed, son of Sultan Murad III, which lasted for 52 days and 52 nights in AH 990 / AD 1582. It documents, in both word and image, how during the festivities the craft guilds paraded their various products, how a variety of entertainments were organised, how banquets were held and food distributed to the public every day, how the sultan would scatter gold and silver among the people from time to time, how poor children were circumcised and given new clothes, how beggars were made happy, and how people who had been imprisoned for debt were granted their freedom by having their debts paid. For this reason the *Surname* is an important historical source providing for us a record of the AH 10th- / AD 16th-century Ottoman lifestyle; its economy, social life, culture, art and entertainment.  
  
The celebration was held in the Hippodrome, i.e. the 'Horse Square'. The Ibrahim Pasha Palace is depicted here, and the three-storey wooden spectators' gallery erected at one of its corners for the use of palace officials and representatives of foreign governments, is an indispensable element of the scenes in the *Surname*.  
  
One of these scenes represents the parade of the glassmakers' guild. Here the sultan, seated on the enclosed balcony of the audience hall in the Ibrahim Pasha Palace, watches the glassmakers' guild along with the assembled people and the guests sitting in the spectators' gallery. The glassmakers present the glass objects they have made, even showing the stages of glass production and the tools they use with the help of a furnace mounted on a wheeled wagon.  
  
Another painting in the *Surname* shows the procession of architects and engineers with a faithful replica of the Süleymaniye Mosque made of wood and ivory. This picture is noteworthy because it represents Ottoman art in all its splendour, celebrated in both the depiction of the architect Sinan, who was still alive in this period and probably participated in this parade, and, through his most monumental building: the Süleymaniye Mosque.  
  
The celebrations of the circumcision festival are transformed into a painted story through 250 double-page miniatures with compositions generally similar to the two seen here.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.short_description: *Surname* is a magnificent manuscript telling the story of the circumcision festival of Prince Mehmed, son of Sultan Murad III, held at the Hippodrome in front of the Ibrahim Pasha Palace in AH 990 / AD 1582. The setting, processions and events are depicted both in writing and in miniatures.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.type: Manuscript, paper, ink, watercolor, miniature painting
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.method_for_datation: Since some pages of the manuscript are missing, including the colophon, it has been ascertained from the Kepeci Ruus register in the archives (3 Safar 997/1583 no. 250, 37) that it was completed in 997 / 1588.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.method_for_provenance: It is known that this manuscript was prepared by the team of artists in the Topkapi Palace atelier, and that it was therefore produced in Istanbul.
72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.obtention: The *Surname* was made for Sultan Murad III in the Topkapi Palace atelier and is still in the palace library.

72c0e86c-b1ae-5017-a60e-32986c29c774.artist:
In the Surname, the writer Intizami describes the preparation of the work in a section entitled ‘Description of the painter and his qualities’, stating that it was prepared by Naqqash Osman (who, like himself, was from the town of Foça in Herzegovina) and his team, although he does not give the names of the members of the team. A document dated 997 (AD 1588) written by the court panegyrist Sayyid Loqman on the subject of raising the salaries of the team working on the Hünername and the Surname, though, does list the names of the team members. Although it is impossible to determine from this document who was working on the Hünername and who on the Surname (or on both), the document is important because it gives a general idea of which painters (naqqash in Turkish) and other artists might have been working on Naqqash Osman’s team. The names that appear in this document are:  
Calligraphers: Seyyid Kasım; Mustafa; Feramruz?; Ali; Abdurrahman.  
Bookbinders: Abdi Şaban; Mehmet Haydar; Kara Mehmed; Mehmed …; Recep Abdullah.  
Painters (naqqash): Osman; Lütfi; Ali; Mehmed Haydar; Velican; Mehmed Musavvir; Molla … ; İbrahim; \[another\] Osman; Ahmed Abdullah; Hüseyin Zergub; Mahmud Müzehib?; … Abdullah …  
Illuminators: Musa Ahmed; Yahya; Seydi; Abdi Zergub; Şaban; Hızır Gazi; Mehmed Abdullah; Mehmed Mustafa; Nasuh bin Abdullah; Perviz Abdullah; Abd … Yakub; Davud Abdullah; Yusuf Abdullah.

74c8d2f0-d499-5753-a385-cea7dbf6cb7a.name: Muhammad Jandarajizada (?), *Muraqqa'* (Album)
74c8d2f0-d499-5753-a385-cea7dbf6cb7a.short_description: This *muraqqa‘* (album) was compiled for the Ottoman Sultan Murad III (reigned 1574-1595) in Istanbul in 980 AH/1572-73 AD. The term *muraqqa’* (‘patched garment’) refers to the patchwork character of the collection of calligraphy, drawing, and painting in codex-format, which was significant for Safavid and Ottoman cultures as a means of collecting and displaying artworks. Likely created according to a systematic and aesthetic process of selecting materials, the specimens of this album were arranged in a particular order. It includes 18 ornamental pen-and-ink drawings, eight figural pen-and-ink drawings, 16 paintings, eight figural lacquer paintings, eleven pages with paper cutting, and 54 pages with calligraphy as the main motif. These specimens are mounted within perforated boards of variously decorated frames. The introduction to the album names a certain Muhammad Jandarajizada as its artistic compiler, while the scribe’s name is Haidar al-Husaini. The dedication to Sultan Murad III can be found on fol. 2b, and it appears that it was gifted to him at least two years after its completion. A red lacquer seal of Franz von Ottenfels-Gschind, the Austrian *internuntius* in Constantinople, on fol. 1a reveals the person who brought the album to Austria as a diplomatic gift for the Austrian emperor, after which it became part of the Austrian National Library in 1833-34.
74c8d2f0-d499-5753-a385-cea7dbf6cb7a.method_for_provenance: On fol. 2b, dedication to the reigning Sultan Murad Khan ibn Sultan Selim Khan. On fol. 48b, a cut-out and affixed owner's stamp of a so-called Mustafa as-Selaniki with the date 978 AH / 1570-71 AD. On Fol. 1a,  red lacquer seal of Baron Franz von Ottenfels-Gschind incnluding the name Ottenfels and an Arabic motto in Arabic script.
74c8d2f0-d499-5753-a385-cea7dbf6cb7a.obtention: Baron Franz von Ottenfels-Gschind, Austrian Internuntius at Constantinople, donated the album to the Austrian National Library in 1833/34.

75805f88-9097-5845-bd37-d89f589785bd.name: Qur'an
75805f88-9097-5845-bd37-d89f589785bd.short_description: The text of this Qur’an was copied in a bold *naskhi* script in Cairo, the capital city of the Mamluk dynasty (AD 1250–1517), by the calligrapher Muhammad ibn ‘Abdullah ibn Ahmad al-Ansari al-Khazraji. The manuscript’s fine illumination has been attributed to Muhammad ibn Mubadir, one of the illuminators of the well-known Baybar’s Qur’an, now in the British Library. The central panel of the frontispiece consists of a star-polygon design, typical of Mamluk illumination of the time and a pattern that was also used in the decoration of other media, such as inlaid wooden doors. The patronage of Mamluk sultans and their amirs was focused primarily on Qur’ans and architectural complexes, to which Qur’ans, such as this fine example, were often donated.
keywords: koran; calligraphy; script; illumination; geometric decoration; kufic; shamsa; palmette; arabesque; patronage; religious manuscript
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper

75ede8fe-76f3-5385-bdc5-f85fce889190.name: Quran
75ede8fe-76f3-5385-bdc5-f85fce889190.short_description: These are two pages from a calligraphic Quran written in maghrebi script, dating to the 18th century, and a good example of the symbiosis between Hispano-Islamic and Ottoman influences. Although the script and the colour of the diacritics are typically maghrebi, the decoration and the frontispiece of the fatiha, which is adorned with floral motifs, shows the clear influence of the Ottoman school, which was itself inspired by Iranian art. The vowels are written in red, the *sukun* and the *shadda* in blue, the *hamza* in yellow or gold and the *hamza al-wasl* in green.

keywords: Calligraphy; Ottoman influences

76bd886e-d945-5f5e-b0b1-071c229a6721.name: "The Castle Water Clock" from al-Jazari's "Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices"
76bd886e-d945-5f5e-b0b1-071c229a6721.description:
In the early AH 8th / AD 13th-century, a scholar and engineer named Isma‘il Ibn al-Razzaz al-Jazari wrote a famous treatise called *Kitab fi ma‛rifat al-hiyal al-handasiyya*, or The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices. The text offered detailed descriptions of a series of elaborate machines designed to delight and impress the elites at the court where he served, in eastern Anatolia. Al-Jazari’s text and its illustrations belong to a long tradition of studies about these kinds of devices, including Greek compendia on mechanics and mathematics. This page belongs to a copy of the text that was produced in Mamluk Egypt in AH 755 / AD 1354, and was copied by Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Izmiri for a Mamluk ruler.  
  
This folio illustrates elaborate hydraulic clock in the form of a palace gateway.
76bd886e-d945-5f5e-b0b1-071c229a6721.obtention: By 1912, Victor Goloubew (b. 1879 - d. 1945), Paris; 1914, sold by Goloubew through M. Meyer-Riefstahl to the MFA.
keywords: Water; Mamluks; Technical Manuscripts; folio.
materials: Ink, watercolour and gold on paper

776becd1-b151-59c4-9e46-f120b2d7a354.name: *The Nightmare of Zahhak*. Miniature from the *Shahnama* of Shah Tahmasp
776becd1-b151-59c4-9e46-f120b2d7a354.short_description: This Safavid folio once belonged to the so-called *Shahnama* of Shah Tahmasp (r. AH 930-984 / AD 1524-1576). It is probably the most luxurious and celebrated Shahnama manuscript ever produced for a royal patron. This painting depicts the tyrant Zahhak as he wakes up terrified from a nightmare announcing his death by the hands of the Iranian hero Faridun. His scream has awakened the entire palace. The *Shahnama*, composed in the AH 5th century / AD early 11th century, remains a nation epic of Iran.

776d0182-9513-5ff2-a690-04f7b572b738.name: *Tughra* (official signature) of Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520–66)
776d0182-9513-5ff2-a690-04f7b572b738.short_description: Ottoman *tughra*s are calligraphic emblems of the sultan's authority and were included in all official documents, including *firman*s (royal decrees), endowment papers, correspondence, and coins. Used by the first Ottoman sultan in 1324, they later developed into a more complex form that was not easily read or copied. This example served as the monogram of Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520–66). Its stylised form is an intricate calligraphic composition comprising the name and titles of the sultan, his father's name, and the phrase “the eternally victorious”. Its bold, gestural line contrasts with the delicate, swirling vine scroll illumination as ornamentation. This *tughra* served as the heading for a long, narrow document in scroll form, the first line of which is preserved in golden script at the bottom of the page.

Gushtasp puts Isfandiyar in chains  
Folio from a manuscript of *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings)
78bb25e6-fdd2-5c9d-af72-c30e121b175e.short_description: Isfandiyar, eldest son and crown prince of the legendary Iranian king Gushtasp, was falsely accused of planning to seize his father’s kingdom. Not knowing the truth, his father ordered Isfandiyar chained and imprisoned in a mountain fortress. In a later battle with enemies, the king regretted his act and had Isfandiyar released so that he could provide military assistance. Gushtasp is portrayed here enthroned, wearing a blue robe. Blue was frequently used in Persian painting to signify key figures, particularly kings.

7a673124-7bea-543e-8cdf-59c06cdc2216.name: Record of the marriage between the Egyptian governmental official Paul Draneht Bey, aged 55, and the Italian Adele Casati, aged 19, celebrated in Oggebbio (Italy) in 1873

7a6f1e1a-ffd8-5d4d-9cce-388c9f25e887.name: Double page from a manuscript of the Qur’an (37:13-23; 73-86)
7a6f1e1a-ffd8-5d4d-9cce-388c9f25e887.short_description: The wealth and piety of late medieval Egypt and Syria saw the endowment of numerous religious complexes, especially mosques, tombs and religious schools (*madrasas*). The ruling elite’s enthusiasm for building was paralleled by the commissioning of a set of Qur’ans for each institution. In the 8th/14th century, single-volume, two-volume and thirty-volume Qur’ans became the standard formats. The marginal ornament on this bifolium designates a rub‘, or one-quarter of a thirtieth of the Qur’an.

7afbbf7d-ed60-561b-9e5e-eaee7949f848.name: Alphabet Book
7afbbf7d-ed60-561b-9e5e-eaee7949f848.short_description: Alphabet books such as this are known as *elif-ba cüzü* in Turkish and were usually produced for children learning to read and write. In this case, such a fine example would surely have been for a royal or other high-placed young individual. The twenty-eight individual letters of the Arabic alphabet are spread over the first opening of the book, with each letter set in a small diamond-shaped space. Above the right-hand page is a cartouche inscribed with the words: ‘In the name of God, who is merciful and compassionate. O my Lord God, may my task be easy, free from difficulty and brought to an auspicious conclusion.’ Following pages show how each letter is joined to other letters and then, on the final pages, are prayers in Arabic.

7b456f9b-750b-56db-a86f-8e36eccf0b62.name: *Khusraw Hunting*, folio from *Khusraw and Shirin*
7b456f9b-750b-56db-a86f-8e36eccf0b62.short_description: This painting from a manuscript of *Khusraw and Shirin* by the poet Hatifi demonstrates the importance of Persian literature in the Ottoman world. The manuscript contains seven paintings, executed in a distinctive style related to western Iranian tradition from the Aq Quyunlu but also borrowing elements from European sources. This scene depicts Khusraw riding on his horse Shabdiz while hunting. A poem on the final page of the manuscript identifies the sole artist of the work, who completed the calligraphy, illumination, gilding, and painting, as Suzi (“the burning one”).

7bcc1f68-b1fc-5f4e-9ba9-572b00e46c54.name: Qur’anic Manuscript
7bcc1f68-b1fc-5f4e-9ba9-572b00e46c54.short_description: Interlocking circles, often punctuated by circles or dots, are used in conjunction with squares, rectangles, diamonds or triangles to form the basis of intricate geometric patterns. Interlocking circles grace doors and windows, prayer niches and arches as an architectural ornament. Silver and gold jewellery and musical instruments also incorporate patterns based on interlocking circles. With such a broad range of applications, the scale of the patterns varies dramatically. For example, a pattern stamped in gold leaf for the decoration of a Qur’an case necklace can measure as little as few millimetres in diameter, while an identical pattern used in stucco or plaster that serve to adorn the interior of a prayer hall can be exponentially larger.

7bd75a35-d206-5701-b425-b077957ef154.short_description: In 1894, the French army officer Alfred Dreyfus was accused of espionage, found guilty, fired and deported. His family, who were fighting to have him pardoned, won over the famous naturalist writer, Émile Zola. 7c3b1c92-51fd-5856-8367-ca91f32596a9.name: 'Mihr in a Bath House in Khwarazm'
7c3b1c92-51fd-5856-8367-ca91f32596a9.description:
Assar Tabrizi, who was active under the Jalayirid sultan Uways and died in c. AH 792 / AD 1390, was inspired by Nizami’s famous romances *Layla wa Majnun* and *Khusraw wa Shirin* when he wrote ‘Mihr and Mushtari.’ It tells the story of the love of Mihr, son of King Shapur, for Mushtari, the vizier’s son.  
  
In Persian mystical poetry, physical love is often a reflection of divine love, and the beauty of the beloved a reflection of God’s beauty. The beloved was just as often a man as a woman, and although love did not have to manifest itself physically, the sexual ambiguity of works like this was enough to awaken displeasure in more morally oriented circles.  
  
In contrast to the story of Khusraw and Shirin, who clearly have a sexual relationship, this does not seem to have been the case between Mihr and Mushtari. In any event, Mihr marries Nahid, the daughter of the Khwarazm shah.  
  
The bathing scene is unusual. The text explains that Mihr, the central seated figure, is having a knot in his long hair combed out

7dbe5f26-102f-5a9b-a9c9-3dbff17febde.name: "The Clever Hare with the King of the Elephants at the Spring of the Moon"
7dbe5f26-102f-5a9b-a9c9-3dbff17febde.alternate_name: Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
7dbe5f26-102f-5a9b-a9c9-3dbff17febde.description: This manuscript contains seventy-eight paintings and many text folios telling the famous tales of the jackals Kalila and Dimna. Based on the book of ancient Indian animal fables, the Panchatantra written by Vidyapati (Bidpai), the stories spread all over the Middle East where they became wildly popular. This manuscript has a strong flavour of Mamluk Egypt in the figure styles and bold drawings, with hints of Ottoman tulips and Safavid turbans. However, the burnt orange palette and darkly-inked lines have led to an attribution to Sultanate Gujarat where it is suggested this manuscript was copied from an Egyptian original. Its life in India is also attested by a Devanagari inscription at the end, although the rest of the Arabic text is written in a strong, left-leaning naskh-like script.

7e9c43e1-9c01-5ae6-aa4e-69ea000166c4.name: *Shahnameh by Firdowsi* (Social Gathering for Entertainment)
7e9c43e1-9c01-5ae6-aa4e-69ea000166c4.description:
The text is written in verse and prose in six columns in black ink and *taliq* calligraphy on Harar paper. The outer edges of some pages are decorated with the *halkâr* technique, while the chapter titles are illuminated in a style typical of the period. Pages 1b and 2a are entirely covered with miniatures, with the scenes surrounded by illuminated edging. The book contains 32 miniature scenes, each depicting a story from the *Shahnameh* painted in the Timur-school style.  
The volume is bound in black leather over cardboard and is of a similar period. Four *salbek*s are at the corners, and in the centre of the white umbrella on the covers. The outer border panels are decorated with a variety of colours in the *kat’ı* technique.

8267bfa4-2166-51d7-8e12-263939dcfc97.name: Calligraphic Galleon
8267bfa4-2166-51d7-8e12-263939dcfc97.description: The hull of this sailing ship comprises the names of the Seven Sleepers and their dog. The tale of the Seven Sleepers, found in pre-Islamic Christian sources, concerns a group of men who sleep for centuries within a cave, protected by God from religious persecution. Both hadith (sayings of the Prophet), and tafsir (commentaries on the Qur'an) suggest that these verses from the Qur'an have protective qualities.

8310ae72-ca15-52e6-8f0c-5560520c46c5.short_description: This folio was once part of a two-volume Qur’an produced during the Nasrid period in the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century. Although paper had reached the Middle East by the tenth century, it did not become widespread in Islamic Spain and North Africa until much later. Despite its conservative use of parchment, the folio displays many characteristics that differentiate it from earlier Qur’an manuscripts. *Sura* headings in gold *kufic* script stand out in contrast with the distinctive *maghribi* script of the text, and gold medallions serve as ornate verse markers.

8483f56d-4097-5e63-a47a-8a53aa99f289.name: *Hilye*
8483f56d-4097-5e63-a47a-8a53aa99f289.short_description: Despite the steady advance of western-style artworks, traditional Ottoman arts and crafts did not disappear entirely. This hilye or word portrait of the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) has been rendered on tripartite, foldable cardboard, decorated on the outside with elaborate ebru paper marbling. Its composition follows a layout current since the 11th/17th century when it was devised by the famous Ottoman calligrapher Hafiz Osman (1052-1110 H/1642-1698CE). Traditionally, the hilye presents Hadith recounting the noble physical and spiritual attributes of the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), often embellished with rich illumination. A large oval cartouche, with the hadith in black naskhi, appears in the centre, surrounded by four roundels naming the four rightly-guided caliphs Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali. Above the cartouche, the Bismillah is written in thuluth style. Below, a verse from the Holy Qur'an (68:4) is followed by the last lines of the hadith, a prayer, the names of the artist and two individuals certifying his work, and the date. All calligraphic elements are set against a stippled gold background enhanced with European-style floral elements.

84a2af32-23c5-5782-9961-db81e133a30a.name: "The Hare, the Lion, and the Well"
84a2af32-23c5-5782-9961-db81e133a30a.alternate_name: Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
84a2af32-23c5-5782-9961-db81e133a30a.description: This manuscript contains seventy-eight paintings and many text folios telling the famous tales of the jackals Kalila and Dimna. Based on the book of ancient Indian animal fables, the Panchatantra written by Vidyapati (Bidpai), the stories spread all over the Middle East where they became wildly popular. This manuscript has a strong flavour of Mamluk Egypt in the figure styles and bold drawings, with hints of Ottoman tulips and Safavid turbans. However, the burnt orange palette and darkly-inked lines have led to an attribution to Sultanate Gujarat where it is suggested this manuscript was copied from an Egyptian original. Its life in India is also attested by a Devanagari inscription at the end, although the rest of the Arabic text is written in a strong, left-leaning naskh-like script.
